claims.text: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 has a single-phase FCC matrix in its starting state.
The starting alloy contains a high density of process-induced dislocations.
High-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and stability of a dual oxide scale.
The proposed dual scale consists of an outer Cr-rich oxide and an inner Al2O3 layer.
The outer Cr-rich oxide forms rapidly and is less adherent.
The Al2O3 layer develops more slowly, adheres to the substrate, and provides protection.
An oxidizing atmosphere favors formation of a coherent protective oxide bilayer.
A reducing atmosphere retards or alters oxide formation, compromises scale integrity, and accelerates degradation.
Process-induced dislocation networks may provide diffusion pathways for Al and Cr and thereby influence scale-growth kinetics.
Synergistic elemental effects cause Cr to oxidize first, followed by slower formation of stable Al2O3.
The layered scale formed under oxidizing conditions preserves the alloy's strength and fatigue resistance.
Under oxidizing exposure, the specimens will show a well-defined bilayer scale, minimal spallation, and superior retained mechanical integrity.
Under reducing exposure, the scale will be thinner, less adherent, or lower in Al2O3 and the specimens will exhibit greater surface and mechanical degradation.
The as-manufactured baseline has minimal pre-existing oxide and beneficial dislocation structures.
Exposure at 900–1000 °C for 50–100 hours is below the thresholds for phase instability or bulk melting in this alloy.
Local Ti or Cr variations can affect oxide-scale nucleation and growth kinetics.
Differences in additive-manufacturing parameters may change the role of dislocation density in oxide-forming-element diffusion.
